objectives.text: Keep the succession inside Talon's coalition. Romuald Wadagni, his finance minister, won the April 2026 presidential election in the first round with about 94% (provisional), since Talon was barred by term limits. The main opposition party fielded no candidate, and the January 2026 parliamentary vote gave Talon's two allied parties all 109 seats in the National Assembly.

objectives.text: Keep the north and the Niger corridor open. Jihadist attacks from Burkina Faso killed dozens of Beninese soldiers in 2025, and the Niger pipeline's outlet at Sèmè-Kpodji depends on the border. Benin enforced ECOWAS sanctions on Niger after the 2023 coup; on 2 June 2026 President Wadagni went to Niamey, and both leaders agreed an expert committee, given 15 days, to prepare the border's reopening.

paradoxes.text: Benin squeezed Niger over the pipeline and the border, and in June 2026 it reopened talks because jihadist violence on both sides of the border made the squeeze costly. A June 2026 analysis reads the jihadist threat as at least as much a cause of the thaw as economic need.

grand_strategy.reading: Benin's grand strategy is to hold a Talon-backed succession at home and to keep its north and its oil and transit outlet open against a jihadist belt that now reaches from Burkina Faso. It treats Niger as a rival it can squeeze with the border and the pipeline, and it reopens to Niger when the jihadist threat makes the squeeze costly, which is the paradox of the 2026 thaw. France and Rwanda are security partners it needs but cannot lean on openly: the French link is under street pressure, and the Rwandan training is confirmed only as an agreement from 2022-23.

stances.note: Rival, not adversary. The border has been shut since Niger's July 2023 coup; Benin enforced ECOWAS sanctions on the junta and Niamey kept the border closed after they were lifted; in 2024 Benin blocked Niger's crude loading until Niger reopened its side. Warming: on 2 June 2026 Wadagni went to Niamey and both leaders committed to reopening the border through an expert committee given 15 days. The sources describe a trade and pipeline dispute with no declared aim of the other state's end, so rival. Bond none: no kinship or affinity is named. Gap: the reported accusations of French bases in Benin are not sourced in this pass; the outcome of the expert committee and any Tiani visit are not verified.

stances.note: Benin keeps military ties with France while the street resists them: in January-February 2025, after the jihadist attack in the north, students in Cotonou demanded the withdrawal of French troops and blamed France. In December 2025, French special forces were reportedly deployed to support the Beninese army in defeating the coup attempt; the French government acknowledged surveillance, observation and logistics support (French parliamentary written question, read from a search summary, not opened). A fact-check reports that France ended its military engagement in West Africa in July 2025, which sits uneasily with those reports. reluctant_partner is our reading; no source uses the word. Bond grievance: the anti-French protests are the open wound. Gap: the status of French forces in Benin in 2026 is not verified.

relations_from.summary: JNIM attacks in northern Benin rose sharply in 2025: an 8 January assault on the Point Triple base killed at least 28 soldiers and an attack on 17 April killed at least 54 (government toll, as reported). ACLED says JNIM uses Tapoa and Kompienga provinces in Burkina Faso as staging grounds for incursions into Benin. The Burkina state is not named as responsible; this row records the spillover, not a Burkinabe act.
relations_from.note: Counts differ by source (ADF Magazine reports 30 soldiers for January, ACLED 34). The 17 April toll is from a summary of the government's announcement, not opened.
